#SupplyChainAttack #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
One monitoring script. About $2.5 million traced to an attacker wallet. 💸

What happened at Polymarket (via BleepingComputer, 29 Oct):
→ Hackers compromised DebugBear, a website performance-monitoring service, and its embed served crypto-draining JavaScript
→ The script checked if visitors were logged in, then tried to use their sessions to sell positions or send tokens to an attacker wallet
→ Polymarket went cancel-only at 2:05 p.m. ET; trading resumed about an hour later
→ About $2.5M was traced to a suspected attacker wallet (traced, not a confirmed stolen total)
→ Polymarket says it is fully reimbursing affected traders; DebugBear told customers to remove its embed code

Why it matters: every third-party script on a logged-in page runs with your users' sessions. List them, remove the ones you don't need, and lock the rest down with a Content Security Policy.

cover.sub: Cisco says CVE-2026-76418 in ASA and FTD SSL VPN is being exploited. No workaround that keeps full VPN security.

slides.title: What breaks
slides.body: An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted request while connecting to the SSL remote access VPN. The firewall reloads: a denial of service. Cisco reports no data theft or code execution.

slides.label: CVSS · exploited in the wild
slides.note: Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026

slides.title: Are you exposed?
slides.body: Three conditions: a vulnerable ASA or FTD release, the SSL VPN login reachable, and secondary authentication configured on a tunnel group. Check DefaultWEBVPNGroup too.

slides.title: What to do
items: Upgrade to the fixed release for your branch
Check DefaultWEBVPNGroup, not just custom groups

items.question: If your VPN firewall rebooted at 9 a.m., how long until someone noticed why?
items.x_text:
Cisco ASA / FTD zero-day CVE-2026-76418 (CVSS 8.6): a crafted SSL VPN request with no login makes the firewall reload. Exploited in the wild, per Cisco. Exposed only with secondary authentication on a tunnel group. Patch now.

#ZeroDay #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
No login. One crafted request. The Cisco firewall reboots. 🔥

What Cisco disclosed (via The Hacker News, 29 Oct):
→ CVE-2026-76418, CVSS 8.6, in ASA and FTD Remote Access SSL VPN
→ Cisco is aware of active exploitation (October 2026); attackers and scale not disclosed
→ Impact is denial of service: the device reloads. No data theft or code execution reported
→ Exposed only if the SSL VPN login is reachable AND secondary authentication is set on a tunnel group, including DefaultWEBVPNGroup
→ No workaround that keeps full VPN security

What to do this week: upgrade to the fixed ASA/FTD release for your branch, check every tunnel group for secondary authentication, and alert on unexpected reloads.

items.x_text:
Yoba campaign: fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop apps on GitHub ('GPT-6 Astra', 'Claude Opus') ship a real signed Codex or Claude binary plus a malicious winmm.dll it sideloads, then an XMRig miner, per Check Point Research.

#AISecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
The installer was real and signed. The file next to it wasn't. 🤖

What Check Point Research found (via The Hacker News, 29 Oct):
→ Fake GitHub projects pose as desktop apps for ChatGPT and Claude: 'GPT-5.6 Sol', 'GPT-6 Astra', 'Claude Opus'
→ The ZIP holds a legitimate signed OpenAI Codex or Claude binary named Setup.exe, plus a malicious winmm.dll
→ The signed program loads the DLL (DLL sideloading), which helps it slip past security checks
→ After a long built-in delay it sets up a scheduled task and runs an XMRig crypto miner inside svchost.exe
→ SEO poisoning appears to push the links up in Google results

What to do: download AI apps only from the vendor's own site, block unapproved installers on work laptops, and alert on unknown DLLs next to signed executables.

cover.hook: 13.4 million installs. Every search went through someone else's server.
cover.sub: Socket found Chrome extensions posing as PDF converters, safe search and AI search tools that hijacked the default search engine.

slides.title: How it worked
slides.body: The extensions took over Chrome's default search setting and routed every search through a proxy before Bing or Yahoo, earning referral payments. Some had no scripts at all: just a manifest and icons.

slides.label: combined installs
slides.note: 8.7M from newly identified add-ons, per Socket's John Tuckner

slides.title: Not just ad fraud
slides.body: The final destination can change at any time, so a search could land on phishing or malware. In one test, Predator Search sent six identical searches to four different destinations.

slides.title: Security-themed lures
slides.body: One cluster, 'SecuryBrowse', had 58 extensions and 4.9M users, pushing names like Fire Shield, Securify and WatchTower. 'Bing-Search' had 37 extensions and 2.2M users.

slides.title: What to do
items: Allowlist extensions in Chrome policy at work
Check who controls your default search engine
Check Socket's full list against your fleet

items.question: Do you know every extension installed across your company's browsers?
items.x_text:
Chrome extensions with 13.4M combined installs hijacked the default search engine, routing searches via a proxy for referral cash, per Socket. Posed as PDF, safe search and AI search tools. Most are removed; new ones keep appearing.

#BrowserSecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
13.4 million installs. Every search took a detour. 🔍

What Socket found (via BleepingComputer, 29 Oct):
→ Chrome extensions posing as PDF converters, manual finders, safe search and AI search tools
→ They took over the default search engine and routed searches through a proxy before Bing or Yahoo, earning referral payments
→ Some had no code at all: just a manifest and icons, no permissions asked
→ The destination can change any time, so searches could be sent to phishing or malware
→ Most have been removed from the Chrome Web Store, but new ones keep appearing

What to do: allowlist extensions through Chrome policy at work, check who controls your default search engine, and remove anything you don't recognise.

Telegram for Android 8.6.2 to 12.10.3: answering a voice call could let the caller run code on the phone, per NebuSec. No CVE yet and no reported in-the-wild use. Fixed in 12.10.4; check Settings for your version.

#MobileSecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Answer a call. That was enough. 📞

What NebuSec disclosed (via The Hacker News, 29 Oct):
→ A flaw in Telegram for Android 8.6.2 through 12.10.3 let a caller run code once the victim answered a voice call
→ The attacker needed only a regular Telegram account; confirmed on ARM64 phones
→ No evidence of iOS, desktop or group-call impact so far, and no reported attacks in the wild
→ No CVE assigned yet; NebuSec says its AI code-security product found it
→ Fixed in Telegram for Android 12.10.4, released in late September

What to do: open Telegram, Settings, and check the version at the bottom. Below 12.10.4? Update now. On work phones, enforce app updates through MDM.
